## Goal

Add and run an end-to-end Tonic benchmark that compares the experimental DSA raw bytes codec against a standard CPU raw bytes codec using a mock bytes RPC.

## Scope

- Target crate: `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic-dsa-bytes-sync`.

# Tonic mock bytes RPC throughput — 2026-06-08

## Benchmark shape

Standalone executable: `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic-dsa-bytes-sync/src/bin/mock_bytes_rpc_throughput.rs`.

The benchmark starts a real Tonic TCP server and client on localhost. The service is a unary mock bytes RPC:

```text
client Bytes payload -> tonic request encode -> HTTP/2 -> server raw Bytes decode
server echoes the Bytes -> tonic response encode -> HTTP/2 -> client raw Bytes decode
```

The application body does not do protobuf work or business logic. The standard codec uses CPU `BufMut::put` for encode. The DSA codec uses `DsaBufCodec` with `/dev/dsa/wq0.0`. Both paths use the same raw bytes decoder.

The executable validates echoed payload bytes before timing and checks echoed length during the timed loop. Throughput uses concurrent unary RPCs over Tonic `Channel` clones. The server accepts sockets with `TCP_NODELAY` and shuts each per-row server down after measurement.

## Command

Built from `accel-rpc/tonic`:

```bash
cargo build --release -p tonic-dsa-bytes-sync --bin mock_bytes_rpc_throughput
```

Ran from repo root through the DSA launcher so the process has `CAP_SYS_RAWIO`:

```bash
launch accel-rpc/tonic/target/release/mock_bytes_rpc_throughput \
  --codec both \
  --requests 5000 \
  --concurrency 64 \
  --warmup 256 \
  --dsa-wq /dev/dsa/wq0.0
```

## Results

Run 1:

| codec | payload bytes | requests | concurrency | elapsed ms | requests/s | one-way MiB/s | round-trip MiB/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| standard | 4096 | 5000 | 64 | 225.286 | 22194.02 | 86.70 | 173.39 |
| standard | 65536 | 5000 | 64 | 426.645 | 11719.35 | 732.46 | 1464.92 |
| standard | 1048576 | 5000 | 64 | 5714.768 | 874.93 | 874.93 | 1749.85 |
| dsa | 4096 | 5000 | 64 | 222.504 | 22471.53 | 87.78 | 175.56 |
| dsa | 65536 | 5000 | 64 | 445.808 | 11215.59 | 700.97 | 1401.95 |
| dsa | 1048576 | 5000 | 64 | 4550.614 | 1098.75 | 1098.75 | 2197.51 |

Run 2:

| codec | payload bytes | requests | concurrency | elapsed ms | requests/s | one-way MiB/s | round-trip MiB/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| standard | 4096 | 5000 | 64 | 216.996 | 23041.94 | 90.01 | 180.02 |
| standard | 65536 | 5000 | 64 | 428.862 | 11658.76 | 728.67 | 1457.34 |

Run 3:

| codec | payload bytes | requests | concurrency | elapsed ms | requests/s | one-way MiB/s | round-trip MiB/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| standard | 4096 | 5000 | 64 | 224.696 | 22252.27 | 86.92 | 173.85 |
| standard | 65536 | 5000 | 64 | 433.806 | 11525.89 | 720.37 | 1440.74 |

| payload bytes | standard req/s | dsa req/s | dsa / standard | standard one-way MiB/s | dsa one-way MiB/s |

## Smaller payload follow-up

Follow-up command:

```bash
launch accel-rpc/tonic/target/release/mock_bytes_rpc_throughput \
  --codec both \
  --payload-bytes 64 \
  --payload-bytes 256 \
  --payload-bytes 1024 \
  --payload-bytes 2048 \
  --payload-bytes 4096 \
  --requests 50000 \
```

The earlier 20k-request sweep over the same small sizes had the same broad shape for sub-1 KiB payloads but was noisier around 2 KiB and 4 KiB.

## Crossover follow-up

Forced-DSA (`--dsa-min-message-bytes 1`) sweeps were noisy below 1 MiB. Single runs alternated between DSA wins and losses at 16 KiB through 512 KiB, so there is no stable crossover in that range from this end-to-end benchmark.

Larger payloads were more consistent. Average of two 2k-request runs:

| payload bytes | standard one-way MiB/s | dsa one-way MiB/s | dsa / standard |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1048576 | 1212.00 | 1226.22 | 1.01x |
| 2097152 | 1017.84 | 1151.62 | 1.13x |
| 4194304 | 1083.27 | 1302.37 | 1.20x |

A threshold-policy run with `--dsa-min-message-bytes 1048576` preserved CPU fallback below 1 MiB and showed DSA wins at 1 MiB, 2 MiB, and 4 MiB in that run. Because the below-threshold rows still showed ordinary run-to-run variance, this should be treated as policy validation, not as a precise crossover measurement.

## Isolated encoder check

The isolated encoder benchmark confirms the expected hardware-copy behavior: DSA is slower than CPU copy for small and medium messages when measuring only the encode copy path.

Command:

```bash
TONIC_DSA_WQ=/dev/dsa/wq0.0 launch bash -lc 'cd accel-rpc/tonic && cargo bench -p tonic-dsa-bytes-sync --bench buf_codec'
```

Observed:

| payload | software ns/iter | DSA ns/iter | DSA / software |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 KiB | 123 | 1402 | 11.40x slower |
| 64 KiB | 1483 | 3523 | 2.38x slower |
| 1 MiB | 33340 | 37470 | 1.12x slower |

This means the small-message e2e rows must not be interpreted as DSA hardware being faster for tiny copies. The copy itself is slower; framework scheduling, h2/Tonic overhead, allocator behavior, and run-to-run variance dominate the small-message e2e measurements.

## Profiling follow-up

Profiles were collected with `perf record -F 199 -g` through `launch`.

Small payload, 64 B:

| codec | req/s under perf | dominant flat samples |
|---|---:|---|
| standard | 39165.36 | `std::sys::sync::mutex::futex::Mutex::lock_contended` 30.80%, Tokio scheduler ~6.4%, `__memmove_avx512_unaligned_erms` 1.73% |
| dsa | 29787.36 | `std::sys::sync::mutex::futex::Mutex::lock_contended` 29.92%, Tokio scheduler ~6.3%, `DsaOperation::poll` 1.21%, DSA encode closure 0.91%, `__memmove_avx512_unaligned_erms` 1.88% |

For 64 B, the profile is dominated by RPC/runtime synchronization, not copying. DSA-specific work appears but is small relative to Tonic/h2/Tokio overhead; under profiling, forced DSA was slower.

Large payload, 4 MiB:

| codec | req/s under perf | dominant flat samples |
|---|---:|---|
| standard | 314.37 | `__memmove_avx512_unaligned_erms` 49.66%, `bytes::bytes_mut::shared_v_drop` 5.72%, `realloc` 3.50% |
| dsa | 277.37 | `__memmove_avx512_unaligned_erms` 29.66%, DSA encode closure 10.59%, `DsaOperation::poll` 2.53%, `bytes::bytes_mut::shared_v_drop` 7.31% |

For 4 MiB, the profile shifts from CPU memcpy toward DSA encode/poll work, but `memmove` remains significant because not every copy in the RPC path is replaced by DSA.

## Takeaway

At concurrency 64 in this mock bytes RPC benchmark, DSA is not meaningfully beneficial for small payloads. The isolated copy path is slower through at least 1 MiB, and the e2e small-message results are dominated by framework overhead and variance. In the e2e mock RPC, benefits become more plausible around 1 MiB and are more consistent in the 2–4 MiB range. A defensible policy from the current evidence is to leave small payloads on CPU and only try DSA at roughly 1 MiB or larger until a broader, lower-variance sweep says otherwise.

1:# Tonic Interception Points for `accel-rpc`
2:
3:**Date**: 2026-03-30
4:**Scope**: `accel-rpc/tonic` and surrounding `accel-rpc` integration crates
5:
6:## Executive Summary
7:
8:For this repository, the word **intercept** maps to four different mechanisms inside tonic:
9:
10:1. **gRPC interceptors** for request metadata and early rejection,
11:2. **Tower layers/services** for whole-request and whole-response wrapping,
12:3. **transport builders/connectors** for connection setup and protocol tuning,
13:4. **codec/body boundaries** for actual payload bytes, framing, compression, and buffer movement.
14:
15:The main conclusion is:
16:
17:- **If the goal is payload-path work, use codec/body hooks first.**
18:- **If the goal is cross-cutting request/response wrapping, use Tower layers.**
19:- **If the goal is ergonomic adoption, wire those hooks in through `tonic-build`.**
20:- **Do not treat tonic interceptors as payload hooks.** They are intentionally metadata-only.
21:
22:That means the best fit for this repo remains:
23:
24:- `accel-codec/` at codec/body boundaries,
25:- `accel-middleware/` at Tower layer boundaries,
26:- `dsa-ffi/` under copy/checksum-oriented payload transforms,
27:- `iax-ffi/` under compression/decompression boundaries,
28:- `tonic-build` only as the mechanism that makes those real hooks easier to adopt.
29:
30:This report complements `docs/report/architecture/002.tonic_component_analysis.md` by narrowing from general offloadability to **concrete interception points**.
31:
32:## 1. End-to-End Map: Where Interception Can Happen
33:
34:### 1.1 Generated client path
35:
36:The generated client surface in `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic-build/src/client.rs` is the first interception layer.
37:
38:- `new(...)` wraps the inner transport in `tonic::client::Grpc::new(...)` (`client.rs:75-78`).
39:- `with_origin(...)` does the same with an explicit origin (`client.rs:80-83`).
40:- `with_interceptor(...)` wraps the inner service in `InterceptedService::new(inner, interceptor)` before constructing the client (`client.rs:85-96`).
41:- Each generated RPC method inserts `GrpcMethod` into request extensions before calling the runtime client (`client.rs:235-247`).
42:- Generated `connect(...)` goes through `tonic::transport::Endpoint::new(dst)?.connect().await?` (`client.rs:142-151`).
43:
44:So the client chain is:
45:
46:```text
47:generated client
48: -> optional with_interceptor(...)
49: -> tonic::client::Grpc<T>
50: -> Endpoint / Channel / Service
51: -> EncodeBody::new_client(...)
52: -> hyper/h2 transport
53:```
54:
55:### 1.2 Generated server path
56:
57:The generated server surface in `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic-build/src/server.rs` provides the mirrored hooks.
58:
59:- `Server::new(...)` and `from_arc(...)` build the generated wrapper (`server.rs:124-137`).
60:- `with_interceptor(...)` returns `InterceptedService<Self, F>` (`server.rs:139-144`).
61:- The generated `Service<http::Request<B>>` dispatches by URI path (`server.rs:151-177`).
62:- For each RPC style, generated code constructs `tonic::server::Grpc::new(codec)` and then calls `.unary(...)`, `.server_streaming(...)`, `.client_streaming(...)`, or `.streaming(...)` (`server.rs:485-490`, `552-557`, `610-615`, `678-683`).
63:
64:So the server chain is:
65:
66:```text
67:Server::builder()
68: -> optional Server::layer(...)
69: -> generated FooServer<T>
70: -> optional with_interceptor(...)
71: -> tonic::server::Grpc<TCodec>
72: -> Streaming::new_request(...) / EncodeBody::new_server(...)
73: -> hyper/h2 transport
74:```
75:
76:### 1.3 Generated vs handwritten boundary
77:
78:The important structural boundary is:
79:
80:- **generated code** decides how application traits are wrapped and forwarded,
81:- **handwritten tonic runtime** performs request preparation, framing, compression, streaming decode, and transport I/O.
82:
83:For interception design, this means:
84:
85:- if you want an ergonomic API, change or wrap **codegen**;
86:- if you want to touch payload bytes, change or wrap the **runtime**.
87:
88:## 2. Interception Taxonomy
89:
90:## 2.1 Codec/body boundary — best hook for payload work
91:
92:The strongest payload interception point lives in the client/server runtime and codec code.
93:
94:### Client-side anchors
95:
96:In `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/client/grpc.rs`, the runtime client turns an outbound request stream into an encoded HTTP body:
97:
98:- `Grpc::streaming(...)` maps the request stream into `EncodeBody::new_client(...)` (`client/grpc.rs:297-305`),
99:- wraps it in tonic `Body` (`client/grpc.rs:306`),
100:- prepares headers and URI (`client/grpc.rs:308`, `372-391`),
101:- then calls the inner service (`client/grpc.rs:310-314`).
102:
103:On the response path it creates `Streaming::new_response(...)` (`client/grpc.rs:353-361`).
104:
105:### Server-side anchors
106:
107:In `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/server/grpc.rs`:
108:
109:- unary requests become `Streaming::new_request(...)` in `map_request_unary(...)` (`server/grpc.rs:376-381`),
110:- streaming requests become `Streaming::new_request(...)` in `map_request_streaming(...)` (`server/grpc.rs:407-413`),
111:- outbound responses become `EncodeBody::new_server(...)` in `map_response(...)` (`server/grpc.rs:447-453`).
112:
113:### Byte-level anchors
114:
115:`accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/codec/encode.rs` shows the exact outbound sequence:
116:
117:- reserve the 5-byte gRPC header (`encode.rs:145-150`),
118:- encode the message (`encode.rs:155-157`, `172-174`),
119:- optionally compress (`encode.rs:152-170`),
120:- write the frame header (`encode.rs:177-205`).
121:
122:`accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/codec/decode.rs` shows the inbound mirror:
123:
124:- read compression flag and frame length (`decode.rs:152-205`),
125:- accumulate message bytes,
126:- optionally decompress (`decode.rs:214-245`),
127:- then decode the protobuf message from the completed buffer.
128:
129:### What this hook can do
130:
131:- observe encoded payload sizes,
132:- replace or wrap compression/decompression,
133:- control buffer reuse and pooling,
134:- insert copy/checksum operations close to the actual bytes,
135:- add tracing at message/frame boundaries.
136:
137:### What it cannot do well
138:
139:- replace HTTP/2 stream scheduling,
140:- change Tower readiness/backpressure semantics,
141:- improve Tokio task orchestration directly.
142:
143:### Fit for `accel-rpc`
144:
145:This is the **highest-value hook** for `accel-codec`, `dsa-ffi`, and `iax-ffi`.
146:
147:## 2.2 Tower layer boundary — best hook for transparent request/response wrapping
148:
149:The server builder exposes a full Tower layer stack.
150:
151:In `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/transport/server/mod.rs`:
152:
153:- `Server::trace_fn(...)` attaches tracing spans from inbound headers (`server/mod.rs:494-503`),
154:- `Server::layer(...)` installs a Tower `Layer` around all services (`server/mod.rs:563-650`),
155:- the docs example explicitly shows `ServiceBuilder` stacking `InterceptorLayer`s (`server/mod.rs:582-617`).
156:
157:On the client side, `Channel` is a `Service<http::Request<Body>>` (`transport/channel/mod.rs:208-221`), so it can also participate in service wrapping.
158:
159:### What this hook can do
160:
161:- wrap full request/response objects,
162:- attach policy, metrics, tracing, and extensions,
163:- wrap bodies without changing generated application code,
164:- centralize cross-cutting middleware in `accel-middleware/`.
165:
166:### What it cannot do as cleanly
167:
168:- reason about protobuf messages without parsing payload framing itself,
169:- expose byte-level compression and frame assembly as directly as the codec layer.
170:
171:### Fit for `accel-rpc`
172:
173:This is the **second-best hook**, especially when the repo wants transparent middleware-like transforms across many services.

# Tonic Interception Points for `accel-rpc`

**Date**: 2026-03-30
**Scope**: `accel-rpc/tonic` and surrounding `accel-rpc` integration crates

## Executive Summary

For this repository, the word **intercept** maps to four different mechanisms inside tonic:

1. **gRPC interceptors** for request metadata and early rejection,
2. **Tower layers/services** for whole-request and whole-response wrapping,
3. **transport builders/connectors** for connection setup and protocol tuning,
4. **codec/body boundaries** for actual payload bytes, framing, compression, and buffer movement.

The main conclusion is:

- **If the goal is payload-path work, use codec/body hooks first.**
- **If the goal is cross-cutting request/response wrapping, use Tower layers.**
- **If the goal is ergonomic adoption, wire those hooks in through `tonic-build`.**
- **Do not treat tonic interceptors as payload hooks.** They are intentionally metadata-only.

That means the best fit for this repo remains:

- `accel-codec/` at codec/body boundaries,
- `accel-middleware/` at Tower layer boundaries,
- `dsa-ffi/` under copy/checksum-oriented payload transforms,
- `iax-ffi/` under compression/decompression boundaries,
- `tonic-build` only as the mechanism that makes those real hooks easier to adopt.

This report complements `docs/report/architecture/002.tonic_component_analysis.md` by narrowing from general offloadability to **concrete interception points**.

## 1. End-to-End Map: Where Interception Can Happen

### 1.1 Generated client path

The generated client surface in `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic-build/src/client.rs` is the first interception layer.

- `new(...)` wraps the inner transport in `tonic::client::Grpc::new(...)` (`client.rs:75-78`).
- `with_origin(...)` does the same with an explicit origin (`client.rs:80-83`).
- `with_interceptor(...)` wraps the inner service in `InterceptedService::new(inner, interceptor)` before constructing the client (`client.rs:85-96`).
- Each generated RPC method inserts `GrpcMethod` into request extensions before calling the runtime client (`client.rs:235-247`).
- Generated `connect(...)` goes through `tonic::transport::Endpoint::new(dst)?.connect().await?` (`client.rs:142-151`).

So the client chain is:

```text
generated client
 -> optional with_interceptor(...)
 -> tonic::client::Grpc<T>
 -> Endpoint / Channel / Service
 -> EncodeBody::new_client(...)
 -> hyper/h2 transport
```

### 1.2 Generated server path

The generated server surface in `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic-build/src/server.rs` provides the mirrored hooks.

- `Server::new(...)` and `from_arc(...)` build the generated wrapper (`server.rs:124-137`).
- `with_interceptor(...)` returns `InterceptedService<Self, F>` (`server.rs:139-144`).
- The generated `Service<http::Request<B>>` dispatches by URI path (`server.rs:151-177`).
- For each RPC style, generated code constructs `tonic::server::Grpc::new(codec)` and then calls `.unary(...)`, `.server_streaming(...)`, `.client_streaming(...)`, or `.streaming(...)` (`server.rs:485-490`, `552-557`, `610-615`, `678-683`).

So the server chain is:

```text
Server::builder()
 -> optional Server::layer(...)
 -> generated FooServer<T>
 -> optional with_interceptor(...)
 -> tonic::server::Grpc<TCodec>
 -> Streaming::new_request(...) / EncodeBody::new_server(...)
 -> hyper/h2 transport
```

### 1.3 Generated vs handwritten boundary

The important structural boundary is:

- **generated code** decides how application traits are wrapped and forwarded,
- **handwritten tonic runtime** performs request preparation, framing, compression, streaming decode, and transport I/O.

For interception design, this means:

- if you want an ergonomic API, change or wrap **codegen**;
- if you want to touch payload bytes, change or wrap the **runtime**.

## 2. Interception Taxonomy

## 2.1 Codec/body boundary — best hook for payload work

The strongest payload interception point lives in the client/server runtime and codec code.

### Client-side anchors

In `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/client/grpc.rs`, the runtime client turns an outbound request stream into an encoded HTTP body:

- `Grpc::streaming(...)` maps the request stream into `EncodeBody::new_client(...)` (`client/grpc.rs:297-305`),
- wraps it in tonic `Body` (`client/grpc.rs:306`),
- prepares headers and URI (`client/grpc.rs:308`, `372-391`),
- then calls the inner service (`client/grpc.rs:310-314`).

On the response path it creates `Streaming::new_response(...)` (`client/grpc.rs:353-361`).

### Server-side anchors

In `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/server/grpc.rs`:

- unary requests become `Streaming::new_request(...)` in `map_request_unary(...)` (`server/grpc.rs:376-381`),
- streaming requests become `Streaming::new_request(...)` in `map_request_streaming(...)` (`server/grpc.rs:407-413`),
- outbound responses become `EncodeBody::new_server(...)` in `map_response(...)` (`server/grpc.rs:447-453`).

### Byte-level anchors

`accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/codec/encode.rs` shows the exact outbound sequence:

- reserve the 5-byte gRPC header (`encode.rs:145-150`),
- encode the message (`encode.rs:155-157`, `172-174`),
- optionally compress (`encode.rs:152-170`),
- write the frame header (`encode.rs:177-205`).

`accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/codec/decode.rs` shows the inbound mirror:

- read compression flag and frame length (`decode.rs:152-205`),
- accumulate message bytes,
- optionally decompress (`decode.rs:214-245`),
- then decode the protobuf message from the completed buffer.

### What this hook can do

- observe encoded payload sizes,
- replace or wrap compression/decompression,
- control buffer reuse and pooling,
- insert copy/checksum operations close to the actual bytes,
- add tracing at message/frame boundaries.

### What it cannot do well

- replace HTTP/2 stream scheduling,
- change Tower readiness/backpressure semantics,
- improve Tokio task orchestration directly.

### Fit for `accel-rpc`

This is the **highest-value hook** for `accel-codec`, `dsa-ffi`, and `iax-ffi`.

The server builder exposes a full Tower layer stack.

In `accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/transport/server/mod.rs`:

- `Server::trace_fn(...)` attaches tracing spans from inbound headers (`server/mod.rs:494-503`),
- `Server::layer(...)` installs a Tower `Layer` around all services (`server/mod.rs:563-650`),
- the docs example explicitly shows `ServiceBuilder` stacking `InterceptorLayer`s (`server/mod.rs:582-617`).

On the client side, `Channel` is a `Service<http::Request<Body>>` (`transport/channel/mod.rs:208-221`), so it can also participate in service wrapping.

### What this hook can do

- wrap full request/response objects,
- attach policy, metrics, tracing, and extensions,
- wrap bodies without changing generated application code,
- centralize cross-cutting middleware in `accel-middleware/`.

### What it cannot do as cleanly

- reason about protobuf messages without parsing payload framing itself,
- expose byte-level compression and frame assembly as directly as the codec layer.

### Fit for `accel-rpc`

This is the **second-best hook**, especially when the repo wants transparent middleware-like transforms across many services.

## 2.3 gRPC interceptors — metadata-only hook

`accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/service/interceptor.rs` defines tonic's interceptor model.

Key properties are explicit in the code and comments:

- an interceptor can add/remove/check metadata and extensions, or cancel with `Status` (`interceptor.rs:18-23`),

- attach request metadata,
- attach extensions that later layers consume,
- reject early before payload handling.

- inspect or rewrite protobuf messages,
- observe responses,
- implement compression/copy/checksum transforms,
- serve as the main payload-path instrumentation hook.

### Fit for `accel-rpc`

Useful only as a **control-plane hint path**. For example, an interceptor can attach an extension or metadata flag saying “eligible for offload,” but the actual offload must happen later in middleware or codec code.

## 2.4 Codegen boundary — ergonomic hook, not byte hook

`tonic-build` is not the runtime data path, but it is where tonic decides what client/server APIs expose.

### What this hook can do

- standardize how clients/servers are built,
- make accelerator-aware layers/codecs the default constructor path,
- automatically attach method metadata or extensions,
- reduce app-level boilerplate.

### What it cannot do by itself

- touch payload bytes,
- replace encode/decode/compression work without delegating to runtime hooks.

### Fit for `accel-rpc`

High leverage, but only as a **wiring layer**. It should make the real codec/layer hooks easy to use, not become the payload implementation itself.

## 2.5 Transport builders/connectors — connection and protocol tuning hook

`accel-rpc/tonic/tonic/src/transport/channel/endpoint.rs` exposes the transport-setup boundary.

## 4.1 First: intercept at codec/body boundaries

Primary implementation targets:

- wrap `EncodeBody::new_client(...)` and `EncodeBody::new_server(...)`,
- wrap or replace `compress(...)` / `decompress(...)`,
- add pooled-buffer management around `BytesMut` growth and reuse,
- add tracing spans around encode, compress, frame write, decode, and decompress.

This is where the data path is concrete enough for DSA/IAX to matter.

## 4.2 Second: use Tower layers for transparent cross-cutting behavior

Put service-wide transforms and instrumentation in `accel-middleware/` when they should apply uniformly across services without modifying generated application code.

Examples:

- body-size accounting,
- request classification,
- extension injection for later codec decisions,
- whole-request tracing and correlation.

## 4.3 Third: use codegen to make the real hooks easy to adopt

The cleanest long-term developer experience is:

- generated clients default to the repo's custom channel/layer/codec stack,
- generated servers default to the repo's layer and codec wrappers,
- method-level extensions are added automatically.

That keeps app code simple while leaving the real work in runtime hooks.

## 4.4 Fourth: use interceptors only for policy hints

Interceptors are still useful, but narrowly:

- attach metadata or extensions,
- reject unsupported requests early,
- mark requests as offload-eligible before the request reaches middleware/codec code.

They should **not** be sold as the payload interception mechanism.

## 5. Concrete Report-Level Conclusions

1. **Tonic has multiple interception layers, but only one payload-centric layer.**
2. **The codec/body path is the right place to intercept actual bytes.**
3. **Tower layers are the right place to wrap whole services.**
4. **Interceptors are intentionally weaker than middleware.**
5. **`tonic-build` is the ergonomic boundary, not the data boundary.**

1. Add tracing around `EncodeBody::{new_client,new_server}` and `Streaming::{new_request,new_response}`.
2. Prototype a custom codec or body wrapper in `accel-codec/` that records buffer growth, copy volume, and compression time.
3. Prototype a Tower layer in `accel-middleware/` that tags requests with method and payload-size hints.
4. Use `tonic-build` to expose repo-specific constructors that install those wrappers by default.

# Tonic + DSA integration notes

## Progress & implementation shape

**Initial framing:** The goal is not to make Tonic/Prost magically zero-copy, and not to optimize Tonic for its own sake. The more useful research question is whether the RPC byte path can expose controlled copy work to Intel DSA, then compare the normal Tonic path, CPU copy path, DSA copy path, and eventually copy/checksum or other accelerator paths over equivalent bytes.

**Hook selection:** The history converged on the codec/body boundary as the real payload hook. Tonic interceptors are metadata-only, Tower layers are useful for request-wide policy, and `tonic-build` is mostly ergonomic wiring. Actual bytes live around `EncodeBody`, `EncodedBytes::poll_next`, `StreamingInner::poll_frame`, frame assembly, compression, and decode accumulation.

**First mistake avoided:** Putting real DSA completion inside `tonic::codec::Encoder::encode` looks tempting, but it is the wrong async boundary. `Encoder::encode` is synchronous. If DSA completion waits there, we either block/spin inside the codec or fight Tonic's backpressure model. The async work belongs in Tonic's polling state machines, or in an explicitly experimental synchronous slice that we label honestly.

## Gradual plan

**Slice 1: conservative Prost encode experiment.** The first plan kept normal Prost behavior unchanged by default, then added an opt-in DSA path that stages encoded protobuf bytes and copies them into Tonic's output buffer with DSA. This was useful because it created a clean experimental seam without changing generated services or claiming a performance win.

**Slice 2: separate experimental codec crate.** The better cut was to move the DSA sync Prost encode path out of `tonic-prost` into `tonic-prost-dsa-sync`. That keeps `tonic-prost` as the clean CPU baseline and makes the DSA path explicit through `tonic_prost_dsa_sync::DsaSyncProstCodec`. This is a good research hygiene choice: the baseline stays boring, and the experimental path is easy to select and delete.

**Hot-path cleanup:** The shared DSA work queue handle should be installed once and cloned into codecs/encoders. Taking a process-global `RwLock` on every encode would pollute the measurement with software synchronization and make the DSA result harder to interpret.

**Failure policy:** If policy selects DSA, DSA failure should be reported as an encode/internal error, not hidden behind CPU fallback. Silent fallback would make benchmarks lie because a run labeled "DSA" could actually be doing CPU copy after hardware failure.

## Design lessons

**DSA is copy, not zero-copy:** The integration only makes sense at explicit byte-copy surfaces. If Tonic already writes directly into the final buffer, DSA may add work instead of removing it. The controlled-copy surface is still useful for research, but we should not confuse it with a production optimization by default.

**Borrowed async codec APIs are a trap:** An API like `async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf<'_>)` would force Tonic to store a future that borrows the same encoder/buffer fields held by the driver. Safe Rust cannot express that self-referential state cleanly. If we go async, the operation should own the buffers while pending, then return them when complete.

**Polling needs real wakeups:** A DSA future that wakes itself in a tight loop would create scheduler churn inside Tonic. The runtime model needs a real completion path: submit, return `Pending`, wake from a completion monitor or equivalent, then finish frame emission.

**Small-message results are easy to misread:** The end-to-end mock bytes RPC showed noisy small-payload behavior, but the isolated encoder check showed DSA copy itself is slower than CPU copy through at least 1 MiB. So any small-message e2e win should be treated as runtime variance or framework effects, not proof that DSA is faster for tiny copies.

## Current evidence

**Mock bytes RPC:** The `tonic-dsa-bytes-sync` benchmark runs a real Tonic TCP client/server path with raw `Bytes`. It validates echo correctness, then compares the standard CPU codec and DSA codec.

**Observed shape:** At concurrency 64, DSA is not meaningfully useful for small payloads. Benefits become more plausible near 1 MiB and more consistent around 2-4 MiB, but the benchmark is still noisy enough that I would treat this as directional, not final.

**Profiling interpretation:** For 64 B payloads, the profiles are dominated by Tonic/h2/Tokio synchronization rather than payload copy. For 4 MiB payloads, CPU `memmove` becomes a large component in the standard path, while the DSA path shifts cost into DSA encode/poll work; `memmove` still remains because not every copy in the RPC path has been replaced.

## Next steps

**Async binding layer:** Build the accelerator binding around the async runtime model first: submit work, hold owned buffers while pending, wake on completion, and avoid blocking inside synchronous codec APIs. This should cover DSA first and leave room for QAT-style operations later.

**Narrow Tonic integration:** Prototype the real async integration at the body/codec state-machine boundary, not in `prost::Message::encode`. The target remains: Prost prepares bytes, Tonic submits a DSA copy for the controlled copy surface, the body returns `Pending`, completion wakes the task, and Tonic yields the finished frame.

**Threshold policy:** Keep small payloads on CPU. Current evidence supports trying DSA only at roughly 1 MiB or larger until a broader, lower-variance sweep changes that conclusion.

**Comparison point:** Intel DTO is an important related baseline because it uses an async-over-sync split model: divide work between CPU and DSA and overlap them. That is not the same as Tonic-native async completion, but it is a useful comparison for whether transparent offload can beat an explicit RPC-boundary design.

## Some thoughts

The main lesson from the planning history is that the agent is more useful when asked to preserve sharp boundaries and evidence than when asked to invent a big integration story. The best results came from forcing small, named slices: keep the CPU baseline untouched, move DSA to a separate crate, avoid fallback that hides failure, run the exact benchmark, then interpret the noisy parts conservatively.

I also think the earlier assumption that "codec integration" automatically means "async DSA integration" was too broad. The codec is the right byte boundary, but not every codec API is the right async boundary. The real design choice is not just where bytes are visible; it is where Tonic can legally return `Pending` without blocking or building self-referential futures.

# Tonic + DSA integration notes

## Progress & implementation shape

**Initial framing:** The goal is not to make Tonic/Prost magically zero-copy, and not to optimize Tonic for its own sake. The more useful research question is whether the RPC byte path can expose controlled copy work to Intel DSA, then compare the normal Tonic path, CPU copy path, DSA copy path, and eventually copy/checksum or other accelerator paths over equivalent bytes.

**Hook selection:** The history converged on the codec/body boundary as the real payload hook. Tonic interceptors are metadata-only, Tower layers are useful for request-wide policy, and `tonic-build` is mostly ergonomic wiring. Actual bytes live around `EncodeBody`, `EncodedBytes::poll_next`, `StreamingInner::poll_frame`, frame assembly, compression, and decode accumulation.

**First mistake avoided:** Putting real DSA completion inside `tonic::codec::Encoder::encode` looks tempting, but it is the wrong async boundary. `Encoder::encode` is synchronous. If DSA completion waits there, we either block/spin inside the codec or fight Tonic's backpressure model. The async work belongs in Tonic's polling state machines, or in an explicitly experimental synchronous slice that we label honestly.

## Gradual plan

**Slice 1: conservative Prost encode experiment.** The first plan kept normal Prost behavior unchanged by default, then added an opt-in DSA path that stages encoded protobuf bytes and copies them into Tonic's output buffer with DSA. This was useful because it created a clean experimental seam without changing generated services or claiming a performance win.

**Slice 2: separate experimental codec crate.** The better cut was to move the DSA sync Prost encode path out of `tonic-prost` into `tonic-prost-dsa-sync`. That keeps `tonic-prost` as the clean CPU baseline and makes the DSA path explicit through `tonic_prost_dsa_sync::DsaSyncProstCodec`. This is a good research hygiene choice: the baseline stays boring, and the experimental path is easy to select and delete.

**Hot-path cleanup:** The shared DSA work queue handle should be installed once and cloned into codecs/encoders. Taking a process-global `RwLock` on every encode would pollute the measurement with software synchronization and make the DSA result harder to interpret.

**Failure policy:** If policy selects DSA, DSA failure should be reported as an encode/internal error, not hidden behind CPU fallback. Silent fallback would make benchmarks lie because a run labeled "DSA" could actually be doing CPU copy after hardware failure.

## Design lessons

**DSA is copy, not zero-copy:** The integration only makes sense at explicit byte-copy surfaces. If Tonic already writes directly into the final buffer, DSA may add work instead of removing it. The controlled-copy surface is still useful for research, but we should not confuse it with a production optimization by default.

**Borrowed async codec APIs are a trap:** An API like `async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf<'_>)` would force Tonic to store a future that borrows the same encoder/buffer fields held by the driver. Safe Rust cannot express that self-referential state cleanly. If we go async, the operation should own the buffers while pending, then return them when complete.

**Polling needs real wakeups:** A DSA future that wakes itself in a tight loop would create scheduler churn inside Tonic. The runtime model needs a real completion path: submit, return `Pending`, wake from a completion monitor or equivalent, then finish frame emission.

**Small-message results are easy to misread:** The end-to-end mock bytes RPC showed noisy small-payload behavior, but the isolated encoder check showed DSA copy itself is slower than CPU copy through at least 1 MiB. So any small-message e2e win should be treated as runtime variance or framework effects, not proof that DSA is faster for tiny copies.

## Current evidence

**Mock bytes RPC:** The `tonic-dsa-bytes-sync` benchmark runs a real Tonic TCP client/server path with raw `Bytes`. It validates echo correctness, then compares the standard CPU codec and DSA codec.

**Observed shape:** At concurrency 64, DSA is not meaningfully useful for small payloads. Benefits become more plausible near 1 MiB and more consistent around 2-4 MiB, but the benchmark is still noisy enough that I would treat this as directional, not final.

**Profiling interpretation:** For 64 B payloads, the profiles are dominated by Tonic/h2/Tokio synchronization rather than payload copy. For 4 MiB payloads, CPU `memmove` becomes a large component in the standard path, while the DSA path shifts cost into DSA encode/poll work; `memmove` still remains because not every copy in the RPC path has been replaced.

**Async binding layer:** Build the accelerator binding around the async runtime model first: submit work, hold owned buffers while pending, wake on completion, and avoid blocking inside synchronous codec APIs. This should cover DSA first and leave room for QAT-style operations later.

**Narrow Tonic integration:** Prototype the real async integration at the body/codec state-machine boundary, not in `prost::Message::encode`. That is not the same as Tonic-native async completion, but it is a useful comparison for whether transparent offload can beat an explicit RPC-boundary design.

The main lesson from the planning history is that the agent is more useful when asked to preserve sharp boundaries and evidence than when asked to invent a big integration story. ## Progress & integration shape

**Research framing:** The goal is not to optimize Tonic/Prost itself, or to preserve zero-copy at all costs. The goal is to expose controlled copy surfaces in the RPC byte path, then compare normal Tonic, CPU copy, DSA copy, and eventually copy/checksum paths over equivalent bytes.

**Hook selection:** The history converged on the codec/body boundary. Interceptors are metadata-only. Tower layers are good for policy and whole-request wrapping. `tonic-build` is useful for wiring. Actual payload bytes live around `EncodeBody`, `EncodedBytes::poll_next`, frame assembly, compression, and decode accumulation.

**Important correction:** I initially treated "codec integration" as if it naturally meant "async DSA integration." That was too broad. `tonic::codec::Encoder::encode` is synchronous, so real DSA completion does not belong there. If we wait inside encode, we either block/spin or break Tonic's async ownership/backpressure model. The async path should live in Tonic's body/state-machine polling boundary.

## Gradual plan

**First slice:** Add a conservative opt-in DSA path after Prost encode. Prost stages bytes, then DSA copies the encoded payload into Tonic's output buffer. This is not meant to be a performance claim; it is a controlled comparison point.

**Cleaner cut:** Moving the sync DSA path into `tonic-prost-dsa-sync` was the right design choice. `tonic-prost` stays as the boring CPU baseline, while `tonic_prost_dsa_sync::DsaSyncProstCodec` is explicitly experimental. This makes the benchmark easier to trust and the integration easier to remove or revise.

**Measurement hygiene:** The hot path should not take a process-global `RwLock` per message. Installing a shared DSA work queue once and cloning the handle into codecs/encoders is cleaner and avoids measuring avoidable software synchronization.

**Failure behavior:** If policy selects DSA, failure should surface as an encode/internal error, not silently fall back to CPU copy. Fallback would make a run labeled "DSA" ambiguous.

## What we learned

**DSA is copy, not zero-copy:** It only makes sense where Tonic actually copies bytes. If the existing path already writes into the final buffer, DSA can add work instead of removing it. For research, adding a controlled copy surface is still useful, but we should be honest about what it measures.

**Borrowed async codec APIs are dangerous:** An API like `async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf<'_>)` would make Tonic store a future that borrows its own encoder/buffer state. That becomes self-referential quickly. A real async design should move owned buffers into the pending operation and return them after completion.

**Polling must not self-spin:** A DSA future that wakes itself in a loop would just create scheduler churn inside Tonic. The runtime needs a real completion path: submit, return `Pending`, wake from completion, then finish the gRPC frame.

**Small-message evidence is noisy:** The end-to-end mock bytes RPC sometimes shows DSA close to or slightly above CPU for small payloads, but the isolated encode benchmark says DSA copy itself is slower through at least 1 MiB. So I would not interpret small-message e2e wins as hardware-copy wins; Tonic/h2/Tokio overhead and variance dominate there.

**Mock bytes RPC:** `tonic-dsa-bytes-sync` runs a real Tonic TCP client/server echo path with raw `Bytes`. The benchmark validates payload correctness, then compares the standard CPU codec and DSA codec.

# Tonic + DSA integration notes

## Progress

The direction is clearer now. We are not trying to optimize Tonic/Prost for its own sake, and we are not treating zero-copy as the only correct answer. The research question is simpler: can we expose real copy work in the RPC byte path, then compare normal Tonic, CPU copy, and DSA copy on the same bytes?

The codec/body boundary still looks like the right place to work because that is where payload bytes become visible. But I think we learned an important nuance: "codec boundary" does not automatically mean "good async boundary." `tonic::codec::Encoder::encode` is synchronous. Putting real DSA completion there would either block, spin, or fight Tonic's async backpressure model.

So the current design split is:

- use the sync codec path only as a controlled experiment;
- keep the real async DSA design for Tonic's body/state-machine polling path;
- avoid changing generated services until the low-level path is better understood.

## Design choices from the gradual plan

The first slice was intentionally conservative. Prost encodes into a staging buffer, then DSA copies the encoded bytes into Tonic's output buffer. This gives us a clean comparison point, even if it is not the final design.

Moving this into a separate crate, `tonic-prost-dsa-sync`, was the right cleanup. `tonic-prost` stays as the normal CPU baseline. The DSA path is explicit and experimental through `tonic_prost_dsa_sync::DsaSyncProstCodec`.

A few small choices matter for measurement quality:

- install the DSA work queue once instead of taking a global lock on every encode;
- do not silently fall back to CPU copy after DSA is selected;
- keep the default Tonic/Prost path boring and unchanged.

This makes the experiments easier to trust.

## What we learned

DSA is copy, not zero-copy. It only helps if there is real byte-copy work to replace or overlap. If Tonic already writes directly into the final buffer, adding DSA can just add extra work.

The async API shape also matters. A borrowed async API like `async fn encode(&mut self, item, dst: &mut EncodeBuf<'_>)` sounds nice, but it quickly becomes self-referential inside Tonic. The safer direction is for the pending operation to own the buffers, wait for completion, and then return the buffers back to the state machine.

The DSA future also cannot just wake itself repeatedly. That would create poll/wake churn inside Tokio. We need a real completion path: submit, return `Pending`, wake on completion, then finish the gRPC frame.

## Current evidence

The mock bytes RPC benchmark is useful because it runs through a real Tonic TCP client/server path. It validates the echoed bytes, then compares the standard CPU codec against the DSA codec.

The current result is not "DSA makes Tonic faster." It is more limited:

- small payloads are dominated by Tonic/h2/Tokio overhead;
- isolated DSA copy is slower than CPU copy through at least 1 MiB;
- end-to-end results become more interesting around 1 MiB;
- 2-4 MiB payloads look more consistently favorable to DSA, but still need more careful sweeps.

So I would treat the current numbers as directional, not final.

## Next steps

The next useful step is the async binding layer: submit work, hold owned buffers while the operation is pending, wake on completion, and avoid blocking inside sync codec APIs.

After that, the narrow Tonic integration should happen at the body/codec polling boundary. The rough shape is:

```text
Prost prepares bytes
-> Tonic submits DSA copy
-> body returns Pending
-> completion wakes the task
-> Tonic emits the finished frame
```

For policy, small payloads should stay on CPU for now. Current evidence only supports trying DSA around 1 MiB or larger.

Intel DTO is also worth comparing against. It uses an async-over-sync split model where CPU and DSA each handle part of the copy and overlap. That is different from a Tonic-native async design, but it is a useful baseline for transparent offload.

## Some thoughts

I think the main process lesson is that small, named slices worked better than broad integration requests. The useful pattern was: keep the CPU baseline untouched, isolate the DSA path, make failure visible, run one concrete benchmark, and interpret noisy results carefully.

For future profiling/report work, I should probably ask the agent to analyze one workload or one profile at a time, with symbols and configuration checked first. Asking for a big synthesis too early tends to produce a polished story before the evidence is solid.
